Evidence package · Gastroenterology & Hepatology Phase 2/3 · starts 2015–2024

PPAR (liver): 2 molecules stopped early, all small molecules

4 stopped trials, but 2 molecules — all small molecules: Elafibranor and Seladelpar.

2distinct molecules behind 4 stopped trials
12.9%4 of 31 closed trials (95% CI 5.1%–28.9%)
4.2%all gastroenterology & hepatology trials with a resolved drug target
1 / 2 own data / decided elsewhere (1 not established)
2independent sponsor–asset programmes behind the stops

What we read from this

  • 4 stopped trials, but 2 molecules — all small molecules: Elafibranor and Seladelpar. A rate counts registry records; those records are 2 development programmes, and the question for an asset under review is whether it shares the molecule, the target epitope, the population or the endpoint of the ones that failed.
  • 4 of 31 closed trials in this cohort were terminated for a biological reason: 12.9% against 4.2% for all gastroenterology & hepatology trials with a resolved drug target, 3.0× that rate.
  • 1 of those stops were the trial's own verdict; 2 followed a decision taken elsewhere, and 1 cannot be established from the record. The cohort is weaker evidence about the mechanism than the count of records suggests: the question to take into a diligence meeting is whether the asset under review shares the molecule, the population or the endpoint of the programmes that failed.
  • The stops came from 2 sponsor–asset programmes across 2 sponsors; removing the largest (Gilead Sciences, 2 stops) leaves 8.3%.
  • 2 further closed trials were terminated with no cause we can read. They are listed below rather than dropped; if every one were biological the rate would be 19.4%, which is the upper edge of the honest band.

Limits

  • This describes registry records for trials that have closed. It is not a forecast for any asset.
  • The rate is not a failure rate: a trial that ran to completion and missed its endpoint is not in it. Those trials are listed separately where the sponsor posted an analysis to read; most posted none, so the missed-endpoint count is a floor and not a rate.
  • Comparisons are unadjusted. Indication, line of therapy, biomarker selection and development era are not matched between this cohort and its comparator.
  • Extraction, classification and attribution are automated. No clinician has reviewed these records.
  • Sponsors differ several-fold in how often they record a readable cause, so part of any difference between cohorts is a difference in disclosure.

Attribution method: A stop counts as this trial's own when the registry text describes a finding in this trial. It counts as a decision taken elsewhere when the text points outward — to another study, a programme or development halt, or a named upstream trial — or when other trials of the same sponsor-asset programme stopped within eight months and the text says nothing either way. What the sponsor wrote beats the structural signal. 'Not established' is a real answer.

What we read from this

  • 7 stopped trials, but 2 molecules — all small molecules: Pemetrexed and Gemcitabine. A rate counts registry records; those records are 2 development programmes, and the question for an asset under review is whether it shares the molecule, the target epitope, the population or the endpoint of the ones that failed.
  • 7 of 176 closed trials in this cohort were terminated for a biological reason: 4.0% against 5.0% for all oncology trials with a resolved drug target.
  • All 4 stops we could attribute were the trial's own verdict rather than a consequence of a decision elsewhere, which makes the cohort unusually clean evidence for its size.
  • The stops came from 7 sponsor–asset programmes across 7 sponsors; removing the largest (Tufts Medical Center, 1 stops) leaves 3.4%.
  • 19 further closed trials were terminated with no cause we can read. They are listed below rather than dropped; if every one were biological the rate would be 14.8%, which is the upper edge of the honest band.
  • Only 29% of the cohort has closed. Trials that stop early close sooner than trials that run to completion, so a rate read this early tends to overstate; the time-to-event figures are the ones to use.

Limits

  • This describes registry records for trials that have closed. It is not a forecast for any asset.
  • The rate is not a failure rate: a trial that ran to completion and missed its endpoint is not in it. Those trials are listed separately where the sponsor posted an analysis to read; most posted none, so the missed-endpoint count is a floor and not a rate.
  • Comparisons are unadjusted. Indication, line of therapy, biomarker selection and development era are not matched between this cohort and its comparator.
  • Extraction, classification and attribution are automated. No clinician has reviewed these records.
  • Sponsors differ several-fold in how often they record a readable cause, so part of any difference between cohorts is a difference in disclosure.

Evidence package · Oncology Phase 2/3 · starts 2015–2024

EGFR: 13 molecules stopped early

20 stopped trials across 13 molecules: Cetuximab, Erlotinib, Osimertinib, Tarloxotinib and 9 more.

13distinct molecules behind 20 stopped trials
7.4%20 of 271 closed trials (95% CI 4.8%–11.1%)

5 / 2 own data / decided elsewhere (13 not established)
19independent sponsor–asset programmes behind the stops

What we read from this

  • 20 stopped trials across 13 molecules: Cetuximab, Erlotinib, Osimertinib, Tarloxotinib and 9 more. A rate counts registry records; those records are 13 development programmes, and the question for an asset under review is whether it shares the molecule, the target epitope, the population or the endpoint of the ones that failed.
  • 20 of 271 closed trials in this cohort were terminated for a biological reason: 7.4% against 5.0% for all oncology trials with a resolved drug target, 1.5× that rate.
  • 5 of those stops were the trial's own verdict; 2 followed a decision taken elsewhere, and 13 cannot be established from the record. The cohort is weaker evidence about the mechanism than the count of records suggests: the question to take into a diligence meeting is whether the asset under review shares the molecule, the population or the endpoint of the programmes that failed.
  • The stops came from 19 sponsor–asset programmes across 17 sponsors; removing the largest (Rain Oncology Inc, 2 stops) leaves 6.7%.
  • 19 further closed trials were terminated with no cause we can read. They are listed below rather than dropped; if every one were biological the rate would be 14.4%, which is the upper edge of the honest band.
  • Only 28% of the cohort has closed. Trials that stop early close sooner than trials that run to completion, so a rate read this early tends to overstate; the time-to-event figures are the ones to use.

This block is our interpretation. Everything else on this page is extracted from the registry and can be checked against the linked records.

What we read from this

  • 11 stopped trials across 8 molecules: Cabozantinib, Capmatinib, Amg-337, Amivantamab and 4 more. A rate counts registry records; those records are 8 development programmes, and the question for an asset under review is whether it shares the molecule, the target epitope, the population or the endpoint of the ones that failed.

Limits

  • This describes registry records for trials that have closed. It is not a forecast for any asset.
  • The rate is not a failure rate: a trial that ran to completion and missed its endpoint is not in it. Those trials are listed separately where the sponsor posted an analysis to read; most posted none, so the missed-endpoint count is a floor and not a rate.
  • Comparisons are unadjusted. Indication, line of therapy, biomarker selection and development era are not matched between this cohort and its comparator.
  • Extraction, classification and attribution are automated. No clinician has reviewed these records.
  • Sponsors differ several-fold in how often they record a readable cause, so part of any difference between cohorts is a difference in disclosure.
Sources: ClinicalTrials.gov (NLM); ChEMBL (EMBL-EBI, CC BY-SA 3.0); NCI Thesaurus (NCI); RxNorm/RxClass (NLM); SEC EDGAR. Cohort rules and classification by Clinical Trial Failures. Attribution method: A stop counts as this trial's own when the registry text describes a finding in this trial. It counts as a decision taken elsewhere when the text points outward — to another study, a programme or development halt, or a named upstream trial — or when other trials of the same sponsor-asset programme stopped within eight months and the text says nothing either way. What the sponsor wrote beats the structural signal. 'Not established' is a real answer.

oncology-microtubule.html:
Evidence package · Oncology Phase 2/3 · starts 2015–2024

Microtubule: 10 molecules stopped early

26 stopped trials across 10 molecules: Paclitaxel, Vincristine, Belantamab Mafodotin, Docetaxel Anhydrous and 6 more.

10distinct molecules behind 26 stopped trials
4.0%26 of 655 closed trials (95% CI 2.7%–5.8%)
5.0%all oncology trials with a resolved drug target
11 / 0 own data / decided elsewhere (15 not established)
26independent sponsor–asset programmes behind the stops

What we read from this

  • 26 stopped trials across 10 molecules: Paclitaxel, Vincristine, Belantamab Mafodotin, Docetaxel Anhydrous and 6 more. A rate counts registry records; those records are 10 development programmes, and the question for an asset under review is whether it shares the molecule, the target epitope, the population or the endpoint of the ones that failed.
  • 26 of 655 closed trials in this cohort were terminated for a biological reason: 4.0% against 5.0% for all oncology trials with a resolved drug target.
  • All 11 stops we could attribute were the trial's own verdict rather than a consequence of a decision elsewhere, which makes the cohort unusually clean evidence for its size.
  • The stops came from 26 sponsor–asset programmes across 23 sponsors; removing the largest (Wake Forest University Health Sciences, 1 stops) leaves 3.8%.
  • 46 further closed trials were terminated with no cause we can read. They are listed below rather than dropped; if every one were biological the rate would be 11.0%, which is the upper edge of the honest band.
  • Only 34% of the cohort has closed. Trials that stop early close sooner than trials that run to completion, so a rate read this early tends to overstate; the time-to-event figures are the ones to use.

This block is our interpretation. Everything else on this page is extracted from the registry and can be checked against the linked records.

Only trials the sponsor completed and posted results for, only outcome measures typed PRIMARY, only analyses typed SUPERIORITY comparing at least two groups, and only a p-value the record settles against 0.05. A failed non-inferiority test is a different event and is never counted here. The rest posted no analysis to read, so this is a floor, not a rate.

Of 1460 completed trials in this cohort, 146 posted a primary superiority comparison we can read: 62 came back non-significant, 59 significant, 25 split across co-primaries. Only trials the sponsor completed and posted results for, only outcome measures typed PRIMARY, only analyses typed SUPERIORITY comparing at least two groups, and only a p-value the record settles against 0.05. A failed non-inferiority test is a different event and is never counted here. The rest posted no analysis to read, so this is a floor, not a rate. The 25 most recently started are listed.

What we read from this

  • 13 stopped trials across 9 molecules: Irinotecan, Doxorubicin, Etoposide, Idarubicin and 5 more. A rate counts registry records; those records are 9 development programmes, and the question for an asset under review is whether it shares the molecule, the target epitope, the population or the endpoint of the ones that failed.
  • 13 of 335 closed trials in this cohort were terminated for a biological reason: 3.9% against 5.0% for all oncology trials with a resolved drug target.
  • All 5 stops we could attribute were the trial's own verdict rather than a consequence of a decision elsewhere, which makes the cohort unusually clean evidence for its size.
  • The stops came from 13 sponsor–asset programmes across 13 sponsors; removing the largest (University of Nebraska, 1 stops) leaves 3.6%.
  • 21 further closed trials were terminated with no cause we can read. They are listed below rather than dropped; if every one were biological the rate would be 10.1%, which is the upper edge of the honest band.
  • Only 30% of the cohort has closed. Trials that stop early close sooner than trials that run to completion, so a rate read this early tends to overstate; the time-to-event figures are the ones to use.

Limits

  • This describes registry records for trials that have closed. It is not a forecast for any asset.
  • The rate is not a failure rate: a trial that ran to completion and missed its endpoint is not in it. Those trials are listed separately where the sponsor posted an analysis to read; most posted none, so the missed-endpoint count is a floor and not a rate.
  • Comparisons are unadjusted. Indication, line of therapy, biomarker selection and development era are not matched between this cohort and its comparator.
  • Extraction, classification and attribution are automated. No clinician has reviewed these records.
  • Sponsors differ several-fold in how often they record a readable cause, so part of any difference between cohorts is a difference in disclosure.

Evidence package · Oncology Phase 2/3 · starts 2015–2024

VEGF / VEGFR: 13 molecules stopped early

20 stopped trials across 13 molecules: Cabozantinib, Lenvatinib, Bevacizumab, Catequentinib and 9 more.

What we read from this

  • 20 stopped trials across 13 molecules: Cabozantinib, Lenvatinib, Bevacizumab, Catequentinib and 9 more. A rate counts registry records; those records are 13 development programmes, and the question for an asset under review is whether it shares the molecule, the target epitope, the population or the endpoint of the ones that failed.
  • 20 of 653 closed trials in this cohort were terminated for a biological reason: 3.1% against 5.0% for all oncology trials with a resolved drug target.
  • All 5 stops we could attribute were the trial's own verdict rather than a consequence of a decision elsewhere, which makes the cohort unusually clean evidence for its size.
  • The stops came from 20 sponsor–asset programmes across 18 sponsors; removing the largest (Yale University, 1 stops) leaves 2.9%.
  • 38 further closed trials were terminated with no cause we can read. They are listed below rather than dropped; if every one were biological the rate would be 8.9%, which is the upper edge of the honest band.
  • Only 30% of the cohort has closed. Trials that stop early close sooner than trials that run to completion, so a rate read this early tends to overstate; the time-to-event figures are the ones to use.

This block is our interpretation. Everything else on this page is extracted from the registry and can be checked against the linked records.

Limits

  • This describes registry records for trials that have closed. It is not a forecast for any asset.
  • The rate is not a failure rate: a trial that ran to completion and missed its endpoint is not in it. Those trials are listed separately where the sponsor posted an analysis to read; most posted none, so the missed-endpoint count is a floor and not a rate.
  • Comparisons are unadjusted. Indication, line of therapy, biomarker selection and development era are not matched between this cohort and its comparator.
  • Extraction, classification and attribution are automated. No clinician has reviewed these records.
  • Sponsors differ several-fold in how often they record a readable cause, so part of any difference between cohorts is a difference in disclosure.
Sources: ClinicalTrials.gov (NLM); ChEMBL (EMBL-EBI, CC BY-SA 3.0); NCI Thesaurus (NCI); RxNorm/RxClass (NLM); SEC EDGAR. Cohort rules and classification by Clinical Trial Failures. Attribution method: A stop counts as this trial's own when the registry text describes a finding in this trial. It counts as a decision taken elsewhere when the text points outward — to another study, a programme or development halt, or a named upstream trial — or when other trials of the same sponsor-asset programme stopped within eight months and the text says nothing either way. What the sponsor wrote beats the structural signal. 'Not established' is a real answer.
